video_title: Bitcoin Just Broke the Bear Market! But There’s a Problem?
gist: Bankless weekly roundup: Bitcoin's weekly and monthly closes above the May high (and a second close above the 50-week MA at 76.8K) signal an early bull, even as 30-year yields hit 5.64% despite a cool 3% CPI, raising liquidity-crisis risk per Ben Hunt and Michael Howell. Also covered: Robinhood's Hood Summit (24/7 trading, US perps via Bitstamp rather than Lighter), the BitGet hack and NEAR Intents firewall debate, the Bitwise NEAR ETF, the prediction-market fight heading to the Supreme Court, Vitalik's 'cryptographic world computer' post, and AI agents as a bank-deposit threat.

insights.claim: Bitcoin's September weekly and monthly candles both closed above the May high, producing a higher high for the year and the highest weekly close since early January, which the hosts read as the bearish market structure breaking.
insights.speaker: David
insights.so_what: Technical traders treat higher-high weekly/monthly closes as confirmation of trend reversal, opening runway for further upside in October.

insights.claim: Michael Nato's cycle framework calls an early bull phase, confirmed by a second consecutive weekly close above the 50-week moving average (76.8K), with the latest close around 84.5K.
insights.speaker: Ryan
insights.so_what: Gives concrete levels (76.8K 50-week MA) that act as the line in the sand for the early-bull thesis.
insights.quote: we are in the early bull and we got the confirmation this week because we got a second weekly close

insights.claim: According to Nato's read, if this structure fails after the monthly averages lock in, it would be the first time historically such a breakout has not held.
insights.speaker: Ryan
insights.so_what: Implies a historically favorable base rate for continuation after this kind of structural break.

insights.claim: If Bitcoin is at the start of a new four-year cycle, the recent drawdown would rank as 'the easiest bear market of all time'.
insights.speaker: David
insights.so_what: Suggests the cycle may be compressed/milder than prior ones, which changes how much drawdown investors should budget for.
insights.quote: That was the easiest bare market of all time.

insights.claim: Bitcoin printed higher weekly and monthly candles despite oil at wartime highs, surging bond yields, upcoming midterms and the unresolved Hormuz/Iran situation; David argues each of these headwinds resolving over the next quarter to a year is a bullish catalyst, so being offside is the bigger risk.
insights.speaker: David
insights.so_what: Frames the macro wall of worry as a stack of potential upside catalysts rather than threats; argues for staying allocated.
insights.quote: Any way that this falls out is bullish.

insights.claim: After 50-300% gains over two to three months, frothy altcoins pulled back: LIT down 30% from highs, Zcash down 20%, Morpho and UNI each down 17%.
insights.speaker: David
insights.so_what: Identifies which leaders are correcting; a healthy breather that reduces blowoff-top risk.

insights.claim: David welcomes the altcoin pullback as necessary to avoid a premature blowoff top while noting he is fully allocated with no cash.
insights.speaker: David
insights.so_what: Signals host positioning (fully long) and a view that more pain is acceptable/possible in the near term.
insights.quote: We don't want to have a blowoff top too soon.

insights.claim: The Glassnode altcoin season index got close to full altcoin-season territory, last reached the prior summer, and is now rolling over, consistent with mean reversion.
insights.speaker: Ryan
insights.so_what: Altseason index near extremes historically precedes cooling; useful timing gauge for rotation.

insights.claim: 96% of the top 50 crypto assets (all but roughly one) outperformed Bitcoin over the prior 30 days.
insights.speaker: Ryan
insights.so_what: Extreme breadth of alt outperformance often marks a local froth peak and suggests rotation back toward BTC.
insights.quote: 96% of the top 50 crypto assets actually beat Bitcoin over the last 30 days

themes.theme: Bond yield spike amid cool inflation

insights.claim: CPI came in at 3% annualized versus roughly 3.3% expected, with July revised down, and the hosts attribute much of the residual inflation to high energy costs.
insights.speaker: Ryan
insights.so_what: A soft inflation print that would normally support lower long-end yields and risk assets.

insights.claim: Despite the cool inflation print, long-end yields accelerated higher at the fastest pace in weeks: the 30-year hit 5.64%, its highest since 2002, and the 10-year reached 5.3%.
insights.speaker: Ryan
insights.so_what: A divergence between inflation and yields signals something other than inflation (fiscal, supply, credibility) is driving the bond market.

insights.claim: Ben Hunt argued the 10- and 30-year move is not oil- or Iran-related (oil fell that week) and warned that something in the financial world is going to break; the concern is the speed of the move more than the level.
insights.speaker: Ryan
insights.so_what: Velocity of yield moves is what blows up levered positions; watch for a credit or fund accident.
insights.quote: Something in the financial world is going to break.

insights.claim: Ryan suggests Treasury Secretary Bessent's talk of buying the long end and intervening is itself evidence that officials see stress in the bond market.
insights.speaker: Ryan
insights.so_what: Potential yield-curve-control-style intervention would be liquidity-positive for debasement assets.

insights.claim: David thinks a violent bond move will hurt someone positioned wrongly (a business or hedge fund) but is not convinced it becomes a catastrophic systemic event.
insights.speaker: David
insights.so_what: Distinguishes idiosyncratic blowups from systemic crisis; argues against panic de-risking.

insights.claim: Citing Jim Bianco, David argues 5.6% yields are historically normal and that sub-2% rates in the ZIRP era were the real anomaly, now ending.
insights.speaker: David
insights.so_what: Reframes high yields as normalization rather than crisis, implying a durable higher-rate regime to price in.

insights.claim: Michael Howell notes 5.3% yields were normal in the 1990s and 10-15% yields coexisted with booming growth in the 1980s; Ryan adds consumer spending is up and the economy is healthy even outside AI.
insights.speaker: Ryan
insights.so_what: High rates need not imply recession; growth-driven yield rises are less dangerous for risk assets.

insights.claim: Howard Marks' memo argument, relayed by Ryan: AI capex financed with debt is competing with Treasuries for capital, pushing yields up as in the 1980s boom, which is only alarming because the whole market is concentrated in the AI trade.
insights.speaker: Ryan
insights.so_what: Links rising yields to AI capex borrowing; concentration risk means an AI stumble could compound a rates shock.

insights.claim: Kobeissi Letter flagged that the inflation methodology was changed this month (recategorizing items such as portfolio management and investment advice), which alone could have knocked about 20 basis points off CPI, possibly explaining why bond markets are ignoring the print.
insights.speaker: Ryan
insights.so_what: If markets distrust official inflation data, yields may keep rising regardless of headline prints.
insights.quote: they've recategorized some things like portfolio management, investment advice

insights.claim: Ongoing fiscal deficits and worsening US fiscal policy underpin the debasement trade, which the hosts suggest is why Bitcoin holds up while bond volatility spikes.
insights.speaker: Ryan
insights.so_what: Long-term debasement thesis supports holding hard assets through rate volatility.

insights.claim: Oil has climbed back to about $93 a barrel, near Iran-war-era highs (the conflict spike was $90-110, after which it fell to about $60).
insights.speaker: David
insights.so_what: Energy is the main inflation driver and a key macro swing factor; David thinks upside is capped as oil still flows through Hormuz.

themes.theme: MOVE index and global liquidity cycle

insights.claim: Michael Howell treats the MOVE index (a VIX for bonds) as the heartbeat of global liquidity; further spikes would indicate shrinking liquidity, which is bad for crypto and the debasement trade.
insights.speaker: Ryan
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete indicator to monitor for crypto downside risk.

insights.claim: Howell's view is that the global liquidity cycle is winding down and the next cycle will start only after a bout of crisis that forces policy money printing, meaning crypto could still dip before the next leg up even in an early bull.
insights.speaker: Ryan
insights.so_what: Key bear-case path: crisis then liquidity flood; positioning should allow for a dip.
insights.quote: things could get bad before they get good

insights.claim: David sees the worst case as a break (e.g., a bank bailout) causing crypto to crash followed by a flood of liquidity, but argues that whenever bond volatility eases, that process itself should be bullish for Bitcoin.
insights.speaker: David
insights.so_what: Either path (crisis-then-printing or calming volatility) eventually favors crypto; timing differs.

insights.claim: At the Hood Summit in Houston, Robinhood announced 24/7 stock trading including weekends, corporate earnings prediction markets, perpetual futures for eligible US customers, agentic AI trading and a social trading platform.
insights.speaker: David
insights.so_what: Robinhood is converging crypto-native features (24/7, perps, social) into a mainstream brokerage, expanding TAM and engagement.

insights.claim: Robinhood's 24/7 trading is enabled partly by tokenized assets on Bitstamp's always-on marketplace and partly by internally matching Robinhood users outside normal hours.
insights.speaker: David
insights.so_what: Shows tokenization's concrete commercial payoff: weekend trading on news events.

insights.claim: The Hood Summit products were explicitly aimed at speculators, day traders and leveraged traders rather than passive investors.
insights.speaker: David
insights.so_what: Robinhood's revenue strategy leans on high-velocity, high-fee trading activity.
insights.quote: It is not for the investor.

insights.claim: David argues earnings-report prediction markets are a legitimate financial derivative on financial companies and should not be lumped with sports or weather betting that society dislikes.
insights.speaker: David
insights.so_what: Earnings event contracts may face less regulatory hostility than sports contracts.

insights.claim: Robinhood perps for US users launched in a limited rollout on eight markets: BTC, ETH, SOL, XRP, DOGE, Cardano, LINK and HYPE, routed through Bitstamp's CFTC license.
insights.speaker: David
insights.so_what: Mainstream US distribution for perps on these specific assets, notably including HYPE.

insights.claim: When asked, fewer than one-fifth of the TradFi Hood Summit audience had traded or knew what a perpetual was, while about a third planned to buy a foldable iPhone.
insights.speaker: David
insights.so_what: Perps remain largely untapped among retail TradFi traders, implying large adoption runway.

insights.claim: The Lighter token fell about 20-30% on disappointment that Robinhood's main app routes US perps through Bitstamp rather than Lighter, which lacks a CFTC exchange license; Lighter remains integrated only in the separate Robinhood Wallet for crypto-native and non-US users.
insights.speaker: David
insights.so_what: Distribution in the main app versus the wallet is a massive difference; regulatory licensing gates who captures flow.
insights.quote: the distribution difference between being in the main Robin Hood app versus the Robin Hood wallet is massive

insights.claim: David expects Lighter to obtain a CFTC license and says the market will know within about two months since the CFTC has 180 days to respond, but warns Robinhood may keep routing to Bitstamp anyway to capture fees even if Lighter offers better execution.
insights.speaker: David
insights.so_what: A near-term binary catalyst for LIT, with a risk that a license still does not bring Robinhood flow.

insights.claim: David is a Robinhood bull because, if every platform converges on a super finance app, the winner is the one with distribution (roughly 50 million customers) and the product skill to stitch everything into a delightful UX.
insights.speaker: David
insights.so_what: Distribution plus product execution is the moat in the everything-finance-app race.
insights.quote: you want to buy the one with the distribution, which is kind of why I'm bullish Robin Hood

themes.theme: BitGet hack and NEAR Intents firewall debate

insights.claim: BitGet, a top-five offshore exchange, suffered roughly a $387 million hot/warm-wallet drain (figures of $351-400 million were also cited) after attackers spoofed internal transfer data; private keys were not stolen, it is the largest crypto exploit of 2026 so far, and users were made whole by BitGet's protection fund.
insights.speaker: David
insights.so_what: Centralized exchange operational security remains the largest loss vector; protection funds matter for counterparty risk.

insights.claim: Stolen BitGet funds were laundered via THORChain and Wasabi CoinJoin, while about $500K attempted to go through NEAR Intents, whose automated shield blocked part of it.
insights.speaker: David
insights.so_what: Shows which rails are used for laundering and which are starting to filter, with regulatory implications.

insights.claim: David argues exchange and bridge hacks have lost over $8 billion combined, so NEAR Intents' discerning, partly trusted firewall is a worthwhile experiment even if it sacrifices pure cypherpunk neutrality.
insights.speaker: David
insights.so_what: Security filters at the application layer may be what makes cross-chain infra palatable to institutions and regulators.
insights.quote: now this new system is more discerning

insights.claim: NEAR Intents itself was exploited for $3.8 million; the same shield limited losses, and users will be repaid because NEAR Intents earns about $3.8 million in roughly a week.
insights.speaker: David
insights.so_what: Implies NEAR Intents generates roughly $200M annualized revenue, a key fundamental for the NEAR thesis.

insights.claim: David stresses that NEAR the blockchain is permissionless and censorship resistant, while NEAR Intents is a separate, more trusted application with no technical dependency on it, like any cross-chain bridge.
insights.speaker: David
insights.so_what: Separates base-layer neutrality risk from app-layer policy when evaluating NEAR.

insights.claim: Base added a seize function to its B20 token standard so issuers can recover hacked assets, which suits tokenized equities even though it is not cypherpunk.
insights.speaker: Ryan
insights.so_what: Seizable token standards are a prerequisite for issuers to bring real-world equities on-chain.

insights.claim: Bitwise launched a NEAR ETF (ticker NRR), and over half a percent of the total NEAR supply flowed into it on day one, a strong debut compared with Solana's.
insights.speaker: David
insights.so_what: Large day-one absorption of supply signals real institutional demand for NEAR.

insights.claim: Bitwise markets NEAR as the intersection of crypto and AI, highlighting NEAR Intents growth, quantum resistance, privacy, scalability, low inflation and revenue-funded buybacks; NEAR has run from about $2 to $5.
insights.speaker: David
insights.so_what: Defines the narrative the next marginal TradFi buyer is being sold.

insights.claim: New York sued Polymarket as an unlicensed gambling business, seeking to bar it from the state plus penalties and payments to users, while a federal appeals court ruled Ohio and Tennessee can regulate Kalshi's event contracts under gambling laws.
insights.speaker: David
insights.so_what: Two regulatory blows in one week raise legal risk for prediction-market operators.

insights.claim: The circuits are split, with states winning the Sixth (Ohio, Tennessee) and Ninth (Nevada) Circuits and Kalshi winning the Third (New Jersey), whose attorney general has already sought Supreme Court review, making a Supreme Court showdown appear inevitable.
insights.speaker: David
insights.so_what: A binary Supreme Court ruling will set the future of US prediction markets.

insights.claim: Ryan frames the fight as states wanting their cut, as with sports gambling, versus the CFTC treating these as ordinary event contract markets.
insights.speaker: Ryan
insights.so_what: State tax revenue motives make this a durable fight, not a quick settlement.

insights.claim: Coinbase received CFTC approval for Coinbase Clearing LLC, completing all three CFTC licenses (exchange, broker, clearinghouse) for fully collateralized derivatives such as prediction markets, crypto binaries and fully paid options, letting it bypass Kalshi as Robinhood did.
insights.speaker: David
insights.so_what: Brokers verticalizing prediction markets threatens Kalshi and Polymarket's distribution.

insights.claim: Vitalik's new post reframes Ethereum as a 'cryptographic world computer' where ZK proofs let nodes verify rather than re-execute, promising guaranteed inclusion via FOCIL, base-layer privacy, quantum safety, 4-8 second latency and light nodes that verify.
insights.speaker: Ryan
insights.so_what: Packages the Ethereum roadmap into a new narrative investors will hear.
insights.quote: Ethereum does not have to be fast enough to do everything only to verify it.

insights.claim: Ryan is simultaneously bullish and bearish on the post because it never names use cases; he believes Ethereum's biggest use case remains Bitcoin-style store of value and associated DeFi, which the branding omits.
insights.speaker: Ryan
insights.so_what: Narrative gap: crypto is in 'use cases season' focused on revenue and usage, and ETH messaging is not meeting it.
insights.quote: world computer for what? For what?

insights.claim: Barnaby from ETH Labs pushed back that valuable state, such as liquidations, must stay on Ethereum L1 rather than only verification and settlement, a point earlier L2-centric roadmaps missed.
insights.speaker: Ryan
insights.so_what: L1 value capture is central to the ETH asset thesis.
insights.quote: I don't want a liquidation resolving on some other server

insights.claim: The hosts lament that Vitalik again failed to explain why the roadmap is good for ETH the asset, hoping figures like Tom Lee will translate it into an investor narrative.
insights.speaker: David
insights.so_what: ETH's asset narrative still relies on outside promoters rather than core leadership.

insights.claim: Apollo's chief economist, per a Financial Times piece, warned that consumer AI agents like Muse, Instinct and ChatGPT's Dot could trigger bank runs by automatically moving idle savings into higher-yield options such as SoFi or 4-5% stablecoins.
insights.speaker: Ryan
insights.so_what: AI agents could accelerate deposit flight from low-yield banks to stablecoins and fintech, pressuring bank NIMs.

insights.claim: The hosts link this to banks' opposition to stablecoin yield in the Clarity Act and expect banks to lobby Congress to block such agents to protect margins, while David sees it as bullish and good for everyone but rent extractors.
insights.speaker: David
insights.so_what: Regulatory fight over agent-driven deposit migration is a key risk/catalyst for stablecoins and banks.
